item.title: 1978: The Cincinnati Reds Dismiss Their Nine-Year
item.description: The Cincinnati Reds dismiss their nine-year, Cooperstown-bound manager, Sparky Anderson, who has refused his front office's demand that he overhaul his coaching staff. Since 1970, Anderson has led the Reds to five National League West titles, four National League pennants, two World Series championships (1975–1976), and averaged 96 wins per season. Photo: grgbrwn (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2023: Gil Was Announced as New Manager for the Charros De Jalisco
item.description: On November 28, 2023, Gil was announced as new manager for the Charros de Jalisco of the Mexican Pacific League. Photo: U.S. Air Force photo/Master Sgt. Julie Briden-Garcia (Public domain).

item.title: 2014: The Royals Traded Crow to the Miami Marlins in Exchange for Brian
item.description: On November 28, 2014, the Royals traded Crow to the Miami Marlins in exchange for Brian Flynn and Reid Redman. Photo: Keith Allison on Flickr (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2012: The Hall of Fame Announces the Players' Ballot From Which Baseball
item.description: The Hall of Fame announces the players' ballot from which Baseball Writers' Association of America members will vote on candidates for the induction class of . It consists of 13 returning and 24 new candidates, with results to be announced on January 9, 2013.

item.title: 2012: Bray Returned to the Nationals on a Minor League Contract
item.description: On November 28, 2012, Bray returned to the Nationals on a minor league contract. Photo: BubbaFan at en.wikipedia (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2008: Red Murff, 87, Relief Pitcher for the Milwaukee Braves From 1956
item.description: Red Murff, 87, relief pitcher for the Milwaukee Braves from 1956 to 1957, who later, as a scout for the New York Mets, discovered future Hall of Fame pitcher Nolan Ryan Photo: Chuck Andersen Delaywaves (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2006: Marrero Signed a Minor League Deal by the St
item.description: On November 28, 2006, Marrero signed a minor league deal by the St. Photo: Bryan Green (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2005: Toronto Blue Jays General Manager J. P. Ricciardi Signs Former
item.description: Toronto Blue Jays general manager J. P. Ricciardi signs former Baltimore Orioles closer B. J. Ryan to the richest contract ever for a reliever in a five-year, $47 million deal. Photo: Julie Rubinstein (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2003: The Boston Red Sox Send Pitchers Casey Fossum, Brandon Lyon
item.description: The Boston Red Sox send pitchers Casey Fossum, Brandon Lyon, Jorge de la Rosa, and a minor leaguer (Michel Goss) to the Arizona Diamondbacks in exchange for starter Curt Schilling. Photo: Cake6 (talk) (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 1998: M. Donald Grant, 94, Canadian Native and Wall Street Stockbroker
item.description: M. Donald Grant, 94, Canadian native and Wall Street stockbroker; chairman and minority owner of the New York Mets from their 1961 founding to 1978.

item.title: 1993: Francis L. Dale, 72, Co-Owner and President of the Cincinnati Reds
item.description: Francis L. Dale, 72, co-owner and president of the Cincinnati Reds (1967–1973).

item.title: 1989: "Barnacle Bill" Posedel, 83, Pitcher for the Brooklyn Dodgers
item.description: "Barnacle Bill" Posedel, 83, pitcher for the Brooklyn Dodgers and Boston Braves between 1938 and 1946 who posted a 41–43 mark; served in U.S. Navy before his baseball career and during World War II; later pitching coach for six big-league clubs between 1949 and 1974 who was instrumental in developing stellar Oakland Athletics' mound staff; coach for 1972 World Series champions. Photo: Play Ball cards, published by Bowman Gum (Public domain).

item.title: 1988: Rich Gedman Becomes the Highest Paid Catcher in American League
item.description: Rich Gedman becomes the highest paid catcher in American League history when he signs a one-year contract with the Boston Red Sox for $1.2 million. Photo: Boston Red Sox Photo Cards (Public domain).

item.title: 1984: Free-Agent Right-Hander Dennis Eckersley
item.description: Free-agent right-hander Dennis Eckersley, on the open market for 20 days, signs a three-year, $7.5 million contract to return to the Chicago Cubs for 1985. Acquired May 25, Eckersley posted a 10–8 (3.03) record in 24 starts, helping the Cubs to the division title. Photo: Rubenstein (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1979: Los Angeles Dodgers Pitcher Rick Sutcliffe
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Rick Sutcliffe, who posted a 17–10 record with a 3.46 ERA for a sub-.500 team, receives 20 of first-place 24 votes to earn the National League Rookie of the Year honors. Right fielders Jeffrey Leonard of the Houston Astros (three) and Scot Thompson of the Chicago Cubs (one) receive the other votes. Photo: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 1973: Al Bumbry, Centerfielder of the Baltimore Orioles
item.description: Al Bumbry, centerfielder of the Baltimore Orioles, wins the 1973 American League Rookie of the Year Award, receiving 13.5 of 24 possible votes. Milwaukee Brewers second baseman Pedro García is the runner-up with three votes. Bumbry, 26, is a combat veteran of the Vietnam War and was awarded a Bronze Star. Photo: Baltimore Orioles (Public domain).

item.title: 1972: In a Blockbuster Intrastate Trade That Satisfies Both Teams
item.description: In a blockbuster intrastate trade that satisfies both teams, the Los Angeles Dodgers send outfielder Frank Robinson, pitchers Bill Singer and Mike Strahler, and infielders Bobby Valentine and Billy Grabarkewitz to the California Angels for pitcher Andy Messersmith and third baseman Ken McMullen. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1972: Robinson's Only Season With the Dodgers Ended When He Was Dealt Along
item.description: Robinson's only season with the Dodgers ended when he was dealt along with Bill Singer, Bobby Valentine, Billy Grabarkewitz and Mike Strahler to the California Angels for Andy Messersmith and Ken McMullen at the Winter Meetings on November 28, 1972. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1969: Second Baseman Ted Sizemore Becomes the Seventh Dodgers Player to Be
item.description: Second baseman Ted Sizemore becomes the seventh Dodgers player to be named the NL Rookie of the Year. Sizemore joins Jackie Robinson (1947), Don Newcombe (1949), Joe Black (1952), Junior Gilliam (1953), Frank Howard (1960) and Jim Lefebvre (1965). Photo: St. Louis Cardinals (Public domain).

item.title: 1967: Foes in the Seven-Game 1965 World Series, the Los Angeles Dodgers
item.description: Foes in the seven-game 1965 World Series, the Los Angeles Dodgers and Minnesota Twins collaborate for a five-player interleague trade. The Dodgers send pitchers Bob Miller and Ron Perranoski and longtime starting catcher John Roseboro to the Twins for pitcher Mudcat Grant and shortstop Zoilo Versalles, who had been the 1965 AL MVP.

item.title: 1967: But Lund Did Not Reach Cleveland Until August 1, 1967
item.description: But Lund did not reach Cleveland until August 1, 1967, and received only a three-game trial with the Indians before being acquired along with John O'Donoghue by the Baltimore Orioles for Eddie Fisher and minor leaguers Johnny Scruggs and Bob Scott on November 28, 1967.

item.title: 1965: Former San Francisco Giants Skipper Alvin Dark Is Named Manager
item.description: Former San Francisco Giants skipper Alvin Dark is named manager of the Kansas City Athletics, replacing Haywood Sullivan, who becomes vice president, player personnel, of the Boston Red Sox. Dark will lead the A's out of the American League basement in 1966, while Sullivan begins an executive career that will culminate in a 15-year stint as the Bosox' co-owner. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1962: The Phillies Acquire Pugnacious Veteran Third Baseman Don Hoak, 34
item.description: The Phillies acquire pugnacious veteran third baseman Don Hoak, 34, from the Pittsburgh Pirates for first baseman Pancho Herrera and outfielder Ted Savage. Photo: Bowman (Public domain).

item.title: 1957: Milwaukee Braves Pitcher Warren Spahn, Who Posted a 21–11 Record
item.description: Milwaukee Braves pitcher Warren Spahn, who posted a 21–11 record with 111 strikeouts and a 3.49 ERA, wins the 1957 MLB Cy Young Award almost unanimously. His only competition for the title is Dick Donovan of the Chicago White Sox (16–6, 88, 3.35), who receives one vote. Only one pitcher is selected each season for this prestigious pitching award until 1967, when each league will name a winner. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1956: The Cleveland Indians Name Kerby Farrell to Succeed Al López
item.description: The Cleveland Indians name Kerby Farrell to succeed Al López as its manager for 1957. Farrell won the Junior World Series as the pilot of Cleveland's top farm team, Triple-A Indianapolis. Photo: Sport (Public domain).

item.title: 1955: The Chicago Cubs Trade Pitcher Hal Jeffcoat to the Cincinnati Redlegs
item.description: The Chicago Cubs trade pitcher Hal Jeffcoat to the Cincinnati Redlegs in exchange for catcher Hobie Landrith. Photo: Bowman Gum (Public domain).

item.title: 1952: International League President Frank Shaughnessy Reveals Plans
item.description: International League president Frank Shaughnessy reveals plans to form two new major leagues by merging the top teams in the American Association and the top teams from the IL. Shaughnessy thinks that in five to six years, Major League Baseball will elevate these two leagues, along with the Pacific Coast League, which nearly has MLB status now. Photo: Goudey (Public domain).

item.title: 1951: The Browns Trade Niarhos, Along With Outfielder Ken Wood
item.description: The Browns trade Niarhos, along with outfielder Ken Wood, to the Boston Red Sox for catcher Les Moss and outfielder Tom Wright. The Browns also sign veteran free-agent shortstop Marty Marion, fired as the St. Louis Cardinals' manager four days earlier, as a player-coach. Photo: Bowman Gum (Public domain).

item.title: 1950: Brooklyn Dodgers Majority Owner Walter O'Malley Continues
item.description: Brooklyn Dodgers majority owner Walter O'Malley continues his house-cleaning as he names PCL Oakland manager and former Brooklyn third-base coach Chuck Dressen, 56, to replace Burt Shotton as the Dodgers' skipper. Shotton, 66, a longtime associate of ousted Dodger president Branch Rickey, compiled a 326–215 record, with two NL pennants, between 1947 and 1950. Photo: Brooklyn Dodgers (Public domain).

item.title: 1945: With Nine First-Place Votes and 236 Points
item.description: With nine first-place votes and 236 points, left-handed hurler Hal Newhouser of the Detroit Tigers wins his second consecutive AL MVP Award. His teammate Eddie Mayo finishes second. Newhouser, a future Hall of Famer (elected 1992), led his league in bWAR (12.2) and bWAR for pitchers (11.3), victories (25), earned run average (1.81), strikeouts (212), innings pitched (313<small>1/3</small>), complete games (29) and… Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1942: The Detroit Tigers Change Managers
item.description: The Detroit Tigers change managers, naming Steve O'Neill to succeed Del Baker. O'Neill, 51, is known primarily as the former workhorse catcher of the Cleveland Indians between 1911 and 1923, and managed Cleveland to a 199–168 record between 1935 and 1937. Baker, 50, a former Tiger catcher and coach, has been at the Detroit helm since August 7, 1938, and led the 1940 edition to the AL pennant. Photo: Charles M. Conlon (Public domain).

item.title: 1938: The Chicago White Sox 25-Year-Old Pitching Star Monty Stratton Has
item.description: The Chicago White Sox 25-year-old pitching star Monty Stratton has his right leg amputated as a result of a hunting accident. Stratton attempted comeback is chronicled in The Stratton Story, with James Stewart in the title role. Photo: Unknown (Public domain).

item.title: 1927: Billy Evans Quits as American League Umpire to Become Business
item.description: Billy Evans quits as American League umpire to become business manager of the Cleveland Indians, following the purchase of the club by a group headed by Alva Bradley, to become the first general manager in major league history. Evans, who worked as an AL umpire from 1906 to 1927, became, at age 22, the youngest umpire in major league history, and later became the youngest to officiate in the World Series at age 25. Photo: Bain News Service, publisher (Public domain).
